claims.text: Abdominal ultrasound is the initial imaging test of choice in most patients without urethral abnormalities; hydronephrosis can be absent if obstruction is early (first few days) or mild, or if fibrosis or tumor encases the collecting system
claims.quote: Abdominal ultrasound is the initial imaging test of choice in most patients without urethral abnormalities because it avoids potential allergic and toxic complications of contrast agents and allows assessment of associated renal parenchymal atrophy. Ultrasound is aimed at detection of hydronephrosis. However, the positive predictive value can be poor (61% in one study of point-of-care ultrasound), and ultrasound is generally not considered the test of choice for the initial evaluation of asymptomatic hydronephrosis in nonpregnant adults (2, 3). Also, absence of hydronephrosis (and false-negative results) can occur if obstruction is early (in the first few days) or mild or if retroperitoneal fibrosis or tumor encases the collecting system, preventing dilation of the ureter.

claims.text: CT is sensitive and is used when ultrasound or IV urography cannot show the obstruction; noncontrast CT is the modality of choice for ureteral calculi; thinning of the renal parenchyma suggests more chronic obstruction
claims.quote: CT is sensitive for diagnosing obstructive nephropathy and is used when obstruction cannot be shown by ultrasound or by intravenous urography. A noncontrast CT is the modality of choice for obstruction due to ureteral calculi (4). CT urography performed with and without contrast is essential in the evaluation of hematuria to assess for urothelial malignancies and other urinary tract pathologies. Contrast increases sensitivity for abnormalities such as cancers but decreases sensitivity for calculi. A contrast CT is also valuable to assess the degree and etiology of obstruction. Thinning of the renal parenchyma suggests more chronic obstruction.

claims.text: Duplex Doppler can usually show unilateral obstruction in the first few days, before the collecting system dilates, by an increased resistive index
claims.quote: Duplex Doppler ultrasound can usually show unilateral obstructive uropathy in the first few days of acute obstruction before the collecting system dilates by detecting an increased resistive index (a reflection of increased renal vascular resistance) in the affected kidney.

claims.text: Diminished urine output, a distended bladder or suprapubic pain → bladder catheterization; without palpable bladder distention and inability to void, a bedside post-void bladder volume > 50 mL (slightly higher in older adults) suggests obstruction
claims.quote: If urine output is diminished or if there is a distended bladder or suprapubic pain, bladder catheterization should be performed. If catheterization results in a normal flow of urine or if the catheter is difficult to pass, a urethral obstruction (eg, prostatic enlargement, urethral valve, or urethral stricture) is suspected. In the absence of palpable bladder distention and inability to void, obstruction can be confirmed by bedside ultrasound to determine bladder volume after voiding; volume of > 50 mL (slightly higher among older adults) suggests obstruction. Patients with such findings should have cystourethroscopy, and children should usually have voiding cystourethrography (see Genitourinary Imaging Tests.)

claims.text: Causes Most common causes by age: children, anatomic abnormalities (posterior urethral valves, UPJ or UVJ stricture/stenosis); young adults, calculi; older adults, BPH, prostate cancer and other malignancies, urethral stricture, neurogenic bladder, calculi
claims.quote: The most common causes differ by age: Children: Anatomic abnormalities (including posterior urethral valves [which occur only in boys] or stricture and stenosis at the ureterovesical or ureteropelvic junction) Young adults: Calculi Older adults: Benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH), prostate cancer and other malignancies, urethral stricture, neurogenic bladder, and calculi (1)

claims.text: Dilation of the collecting ducts and distal tubules with tubular atrophy; dilation takes approximately 3 days to develop
claims.quote: Pathologic findings consist of dilation of the collecting ducts and distal tubules and chronic tubular atrophy with little glomerular damage. Dilation takes approximately 3 days from the onset of obstructive uropathy to develop; before then, the collecting system is relatively noncompliant and less likely to dilate.

claims.text: Obstructive nephropathy = kidney dysfunction from urinary tract obstruction; the mechanism involves increased intratubular pressure, local ischemia and often UTI
claims.quote: Obstructive nephropathy is kidney dysfunction (acute kidney injury, chronic kidney disease, kidney failure, or tubulointerstitial damage) resulting from urinary tract obstruction. The mechanism involves, among many factors, increased intratubular pressure, local ischemia, and, often, urinary tract infection (UTI).

claims.text: Symptoms Pain is common with acute distention: upper ureteral or renal pelvic lesions cause flank pain or tenderness; lower ureteral obstruction may radiate to the ipsilateral testis or labium; acute complete obstruction (eg, a ureteral calculus) may cause severe pain with nausea and vomiting
claims.quote: Pain is common when obstruction acutely distends the bladder, collecting system (ie, the ureter, renal pelvis, and renal calyces), or renal capsule. Upper ureteral or renal pelvic lesions cause flank pain or tenderness, whereas lower ureteral obstruction causes pain that may radiate to the ipsilateral testis or labium. The distribution of kidney and ureteral pain is usually along T11 to T12. Acute complete ureteral obstruction (eg, an obstructing ureteral calculus) may cause severe pain accompanied by nausea and vomiting.

claims.text: Pain is typically minimal or absent with partial or slowly developing obstruction; hydronephrosis may occasionally cause a palpable flank mass
claims.quote: Pain is typically minimal or absent with partial or slowly developing obstructive uropathy (eg, congenital ureteropelvic junction obstruction, pelvic tumor). Hydronephrosis may occasionally cause a palpable flank mass, particularly in massive hydronephrosis of infancy and childhood.

claims.text: Urine volume does not fall in unilateral obstruction unless it is the only functioning kidney; absolute anuria occurs with complete obstruction at the bladder or urethra
claims.quote: Urine volume does not diminish in unilateral obstruction unless it occurs in the only functioning kidney (functionally solitary kidney). Absolute anuria occurs with complete obstruction at the level of the bladder or urethra.

claims.text: Treatment depends on the cause: eliminate the obstruction (surgery, catheters, stents, nephrostomy tubes, endoscopy, lithotripsy, or medical therapy); prompt drainage if kidney function is compromised, UTI persists or pain is uncontrollable; immediate drainage if infection accompanies the obstruction
claims.quote: Treatment depends on the etiology and consists of eliminating the obstruction by surgery, instrumentation (eg, catheters, stents, nephrostomy tubes, endoscopy (eg, cystoscopy, ureteroscopy), lithotripsy), or medical therapy (eg, hormonal therapy for prostate cancer). Prompt drainage of hydronephrosis is indicated if kidney function is compromised, urinary tract infection (UTI) persists, or pain is uncontrollable or persistent. Immediate drainage is indicated if obstruction is accompanied by infection.

claims.text: Temporary percutaneous nephrostomy may be needed with severe obstruction, UTI or calculi, especially when a ureteral stent cannot be placed
claims.quote: Temporary drainage using a percutaneous nephrostomy technique may be needed in patients with severe obstructive uropathy, UTI, or calculi, especially when a ureteral stent cannot be placed into the collecting system.
